masthead_title: Chip and AI-hardware stocks gave back a big chunk of Monday's rally today, but the broader market — and credit — didn't follow them down.
regime_line: A sharp, chip-and-hardware-led selloff — Analog Devices −17%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise −16%, Micron −11% — pulled the Nasdaq down 1.48% and the S&P 500 down a milder 0.50%, even as small-caps, the equal-weight average, and credit spreads all held up or eased, a concentrated repricing rather than a broad one, with today's Core PCE inflation and GDP data due at 8:30am ET.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — one confirms today, one expires mixed

CL-0073 (Thursday 11-19's broad four-way risk-off agreement marking a genuine extension of the selloff, not a one-day echo) — expires mixed/inconclusive. All three test sessions are in: Friday 11-20 closed at 6,910.39 (below the 7,175.83 confirm reference), but Monday 11-23 (7,237.17) and Tuesday 11-24 (7,201.09) both closed back above it — only 1 of 3 sessions below, short of the required “at least 2 of 3.” The index never reached the 7,369 refute level either (window high 7,237.17). Neither the four-way extension nor the one-day-echo read was confirmed; credit (HY/IG OAS) stayed flagged throughout, but price action didn't cooperate with either side of the test.

CL-0074 (Friday 11-20's AI/semiconductor-concentrated unwind reflecting a genuine, still-concentrated repricing rather than a broadening market-wide panic) — confirmed, inside the first session of its 5-day window. Today SMH fell 7.27% (460.18 to 426.75) while the S&P 500 fell only 0.50% — a 6.77-point divergence, well past the 4-point confirm bar — and both Health Care (XLV, +2.95%) and Consumer Staples (XLP, +1.66%) outperformed the S&P 500 the same session, meeting the defensive-sector leg too (Movers, below). The chip/AI-hardware complex took another hit today while staples and health care held up again — still concentrated, not broadening.
story_html:
The story this morning, per quantisnow's same-day recap (“Analog Devices falls 17.3%, dragging the Nasdaq 100 down while equal-weight stocks rise”) and cnttrading's market letter (“Chip stocks give back the Huang rally as money rotates to retail”), is a reversal of Monday's Jensen-Huang-reinstatement rally. Analog Devices fell 17.37% to $312.95 even after beating Wall Street's revenue and profit estimates (Investing.com, Benzinga — adjusted EPS $4.06 vs. roughly $3.89 consensus, revenue $4.37B vs. roughly $4.31–4.32B consensus), with neither outlet tying the drop to anything specific in the print itself. Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell 16.31% to $40.19 despite beating its own earnings guidance and raising fiscal 2027 targets substantially (company release, The Motley Fool's earnings-call transcript, CryptoBriefing), while flagging that operating margin will moderate and that memory-component supply may stay tight into late calendar 2028. Micron fell 11.01% on a sharply cut BNP Paribas price target, $775 from $1,700 (247wallst), tied to memory-pricing worries ahead of Dell's own earnings; Dell itself fell 11.83% to $295.28 in the regular session, then reported record third-quarter results and a $25 billion buyback after the bell (Yahoo Finance, TradingKey) — that after-hours move won't show up in this system's numbers until tomorrow. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.48% to 23,733.54 and the S&P 500 fell a smaller 0.50% to 7,201.09, giving back a slice of Monday's 4.73% and 6.51% gains.

This system's own numbers complicate the “market gave back the rally” read in one specific way: the giveback was narrow, not broad. The equal-weight S&P 500 (RSP) actually rose 0.54% while the cap-weighted SPY fell 0.49% — a mirror image of Monday's gap, now running the other direction — and the Russell 2000 rose 0.57%. Credit spreads, which should widen first on a genuine risk-off day (Unit 3, Concept below), instead eased: HY OAS fell 13bp and IG OAS fell 1bp on their Monday-dated prints, both still flagged on the elevated 120-day trend but moving the calmer direction on a day the chip complex fell double digits. That combination — a severe, concentrated equity move with credit easing and breadth improving — is the live case for today's regime tag and for marking CL-0074 confirmed rather than broadening (Claims, above). Two Tier 1 readings, the 30-year Treasury and the 10-year real yield (the latter's own 23-year record reading milder once cross-checked against the Cleveland Fed's 1982-on model, History below), are still echoing levels last touched, before this run, in 2007 and 2008 respectively — worth holding in mind as today's real test arrives: Core PCE and the preliminary Q3 GDP print, both due 8:30am ET, are the first hard macro data this week that isn't one company's earnings call.
dashboard_interp_html:
Treasury yields were almost silent today while stocks did the moving. The 3-month bill eased 1bp to 4.36% (z +1.82, flagged — higher than all but a handful of days in the past six months; 54th percentile since the early 1980s, 73rd of the last 30 years). The 2-year held flat at 4.63% (z +0.73, below the flag line; 50th percentile over the ~50-year record but the 79th of the last 30 years, † a 29-point gap). The 10-year eased 1bp to 4.91% (z +0.42; 45th/82nd %ile, †). The 30-year ticked up 1bp to 5.30% (z +0.31; 46th/81st %ile, † — today's lead History-check fact, below: before this run, this level was last touched, briefly, in June 2007). The curve barely budged (2s10s −1bp to 28bp, z −1.30; 3m10y unchanged at 55bp, z −1.97, flagged). Why this matters: a bond is a loan, and when nearly the whole curve sits still on a day a whole sector of stocks falls double digits, that's a sign today's move is a stock-specific repricing, not a change in the growth-and-rates outlook that mortgage rates and bond funds trade on.

Credit and the dollar both moved the calmer direction today, which is the real tell. HY OAS — the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies over safe Treasurys — eased 13bp to 3.63% on its Monday-dated print (z +2.57, flagged; 94.5th percentile of its own ~3-year record, marked * since this live series has no multi-decade history, §4F). IG OAS, the investment-grade equivalent, eased 1bp to 0.97% (also Monday-dated; z +2.76, flagged; 84.9th percentile of its own ~3-year record, *). A 40-year proxy for investment-grade spreads (Moody's Baa yield minus the 10-year Treasury, used only for direction and timing, never magnitude) sits at just the 13.7th percentile all-time and 10.2nd of the last 30 years — genuinely tight, which backs up today's ease rather than reading it as a quirk of a short series. The dollar (DXY) eased 0.49% to 103.81 but stayed flagged (z +2.25; 75th percentile over the ~55-year dollar record and the 84th of the last 30 years, †). Gold fell 2.45% to $3,561.90 (z −3.05, flagged) and copper fell 4.70% to $5.36/lb (z −4.32, this run's largest |z| of any series today, Chart of the day below), both extending their multi-week decline. Why this matters: when the two series that usually widen first on real stress (HY and IG OAS) instead ease on a day a whole sector falls double digits, that's informative on its own — evidence the selloff is contained to one part of the market, not spreading into the broader cost of borrowing that shows up in CDs, bond funds, and corporate loans.
history_html:
Today's deepest echo is unchanged from Monday: the 30-year Treasury, still at 5.30%, first reached this level Aug 17 and has been there on 43 of the 69 sessions since — a level the market keeps revisiting, not camping on. Before this run, the last time was June 2007, only briefly, two sessions; this run's high, 5.67% on Oct 7, was last matched in July 2001. The two lenses disagree, itself the finding: 81st percentile of the last 30 years, only the 46th since 1977 — unusual lately, unremarkable across the full record. The then-vs-now panel lines up today against June 14, 2007; the level matches, but the backdrop doesn't — 2007's Fed was near a cyclical peak heading into crisis; today's numbers (credit easing, breadth improving on a hard selloff day) don't look like that setup.

Second: the 10-year TIPS real yield (2.79%, dated Monday) sits at the 99.2nd percentile of its own 23-year record, there on 22 of the last 41 sessions since Sep. 24. Before this run, last reached November 2008, inside the 2007-09 crisis, and only briefly. The Cleveland Fed's longer model, back to 1982, reads milder — 81st/30yr, just 54th since 1982 — TIPS alone are too short a history to call this extreme on their own.

Third: the Nasdaq's 1.48% drop is a size that comes about 31 days a year over the last 30 years — not rare alone — and it's the 25th such day this year; the last bigger one was Nov. 20. Client-ready: the 30-year Treasury and the 10-year real yield still echo 2007-09 crisis-era levels on an otherwise contained day, but what's next to those echoes today is different — credit eased instead of widening, not what those earlier echoes looked like while actually building toward something.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically, plus the top-50 megacaps; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) or a sector ETF diverging ≥1.5pp from SPX, never by seeming interesting. 78 name candidates qualified today and 4 sector ETFs cleared the divergence bar. Earnings/guidance reactions are prioritized per §5; Analog Devices and Hewlett Packard Enterprise both reported their own quarters today and are covered for that reason. Also qualifying, left out under the cap: DELL (−11.83%), TXN (−11.25%), DLTR (+11.18%, no confirmed same-day earnings coverage found despite a scheduled report date — consistent with the rotation pattern below, not individually researched given the cap), MPWR (−10.78%), LITE (−10.52%), FLEX (−10.14%), CIEN (−9.62%), MRVL (−9.10%), COHR (−9.07%), AMD (−8.86%) — none asserted to lack a catalyst, simply not checked today.

Analog Devices (ADI) −17.37% (312.95, from 378.75) — what happened: fell sharply after reporting fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results before the bell. Stated reason: per Investing.com and Benzinga, ADI beat Wall Street's estimates (adjusted EPS $4.06 vs. roughly $3.89 consensus; revenue $4.37B vs. roughly $4.31–4.32B consensus) and posted a record quarter, but shares slid anyway; neither outlet's coverage ties the drop to a specific negative item in the print itself. Read-through: Tier 3-relevant — a beat-and-sink reaction in a bellwether analog/industrial chipmaker, the same day the broader semiconductor complex gave back a chunk of Monday's rally, reads as a valuation/positioning unwind in the AI-capex-adjacent chip trade rather than a demand problem unique to this one company.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) −16.31% (40.19, from 48.02) — what happened: fell sharply after reporting fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 results. Stated reason: per the company's own release and secondary coverage (Morningstar/Business Wire, The Motley Fool's earnings-call transcript, CryptoBriefing), HPE beat its own non-GAAP EPS guidance ($1.43 vs. a $1.20–$1.30 guided range) and raised fiscal 2027 guidance substantially, but revenue of $14.55B came in slightly below the $14.64B consensus, and management guided operating margin to moderate to a 16–17% range while warning memory (DRAM/NAND) component supply may stay constrained into late calendar 2028. Read-through: directly Tier 3-relevant — a major AI-server/infrastructure vendor beating and raising but still selling off on margin and memory-cost guidance is exactly the kind of financing-cycle, input-cost evidence this brief's weekly Tier 3 section watches for, a different angle on AI-capex doubt than demand itself.

Micron (MU) −11.01% (629.79, from 707.70) — what happened: fell sharply with no earnings of its own today. Stated reason: per 247wallst and TradersUnion, BNP Paribas cut its price target on Micron to $775 from $1,700 amid renewed memory (NAND/DRAM) pricing worries as investors looked ahead to Dell's own earnings and commentary on memory costs; 28 of 30 analysts covering the stock still rate it a buy, per the same coverage. Read-through: Tier 3-relevant — Micron is the clearest memory-pricing bellwether in the AI-server supply chain, and a sharp reset in sentiment here, the same day HPE flagged memory-cost pressure in its own guidance (above), is a second, independent data point on the input-cost side of the AI-capex cycle, distinct from a demand-side read. → Route to NR commentary process: today's broad chip/AI-hardware giveback (ADI, HPE, MU, and dozens more) continues the Nov. 5-started AI-capex-doubt theme at the sector level; no position-level view offered (§8).

Sector note — Technology (XLK) −3.26% vs. SPY −0.49% (−2.77pp, the day's largest sector divergence) — Health Care (XLV, +2.95%) and Consumer Staples (XLP, +1.66%) were the two sectors furthest in the other direction, both outperforming SPY by more than XLK underperformed it. Per cnttrading's same-day recap (“Chip stocks give back the Huang rally as money rotates to retail”), today reads as a rotation out of Monday's AI/chip leadership and into retail and defensive names — Dollar Tree (DLTR) +11.18%, no confirmed catalyst found, fits this pattern — rather than a broad risk-off day. Read-through: confirms CL-0074's framing (Claims, above): a concentrated, sector-specific repricing, not one broadening into the rest of the market.
chart_of_day_why: Copper carries this run's single largest |z| of any series today at -4.32, just ahead of IG OAS (+2.76) and HY OAS (+2.57) -- the mechanical pick by rule (a). Copper itself fell 4.70% today, continuing five-plus weeks of decline that have stretched the 120-day average and spread so far that today's own drop pushes the z-score to a fresh extreme for this run.

calendar_note_html:
Today: this week's real test, both at 8:30am ET and high-impact: Core PCE Price Index m/m (the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, cons. +0.3% m/m, prior +0.3%) and the preliminary Q3 GDP print (cons. +3.5%, prior +3.4%). The same release carries the Prelim GDP Price Index (cons. +2.3%), weekly Unemployment Claims (cons. 201K, prior 203K), and Durable Goods Orders (cons. +0.5%) — all lower-impact. Personal Income and Spending (cons. +0.4% each) round out the morning, with New Home Sales at 10:00am ET. This brief runs before all of it, per §4E: it frames what to watch rather than predicting the print. Markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving with a half day Friday, so today's data is effectively this week's last full read before the holiday.

Why this matters to the current regime: today's chip-sector selloff happened without credit or breadth confirming it; a hot Core PCE print or a soft GDP read could change that by giving the broader market its own reason to worry, rather than leaving the weakness contained to one sector.
concept_title: Dispersion isn't a credit signal until OAS says so — today's chip selloff, by the numbers
concept_html:
Segment 4 taught that a violent single-day move in individual stocks or a sector isn't automatically a credit event — check whether OAS, the extra yield lenders demand on top of Treasurys, actually moved before reading a big price swing as rising systemic risk. Today is a clean live case. The chip and AI-hardware complex fell hard: SMH −7.27%, Analog Devices −17.37%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise −16.31%, Micron −11.01%. If that were a genuine risk event, HY and IG OAS should have widened right alongside it. Instead both eased — HY OAS down 13bp, IG OAS down 1bp — on their Monday-dated prints.

Why this matters: dispersion (some stocks or sectors moving a lot) and systemic risk (the market's lenders getting nervous about everyone) are two different things, and only one of them should worry a diversified account. Today's test says this is dispersion, not a risk event — useful to know before assuming a scary headline about chip stocks means trouble for a client's broader bond or balanced fund.
client_translation: A rough day for chip stocks isn't automatically a rough day for the credit markets that set mortgage, CD, and bond-fund rates — today, the two didn't move together, and that's informative on its own.
client_lens_html:
“Did you see those chip stocks? Is the AI selloff back?” Yes — Analog Devices, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, and Micron all fell double digits today, giving back a chunk of Monday's rally. But it stayed contained to that one corner of the market: small-caps and the equal-weight average actually rose, and credit spreads (HY/IG OAS) eased rather than widened — worth saying “this looks concentrated in chips, not spreading” rather than calling it a broad risk-off day.

“Did you see Dollar Tree pop while tech cratered?” Dollar Tree rose 11.18% the same day the chip complex sold off hard — no confirmed company-specific news found, but it fits a broader pattern today of money rotating out of AI/semiconductor names and into retail and defensive sectors (Health Care, Consumer Staples both outperformed, Movers above).

“What's today's big data release, and does it matter?” Core PCE (the Fed's preferred inflation gauge) and the first estimate of Q3 GDP growth both land at 8:30am ET, before most people are at their desks. A hot inflation number or a weak growth number could give the broader market its own reason to wobble, on top of today's chip-specific story — worth checking back once that print is in.
